text: Leonard Adleman's 1994 DNA computation solved a small Hamiltonian path problem chiefly by exploiting the fact that DNA:
choices: Can be programmed directly with conventional machine code
Stores information at higher physical density than silicon chips
Molecules explore all possible paths simultaneously through parallel Watson-Crick hybridization, after which valid paths are isolated by biochemical filtering
Replicates faster than any electronic computer can perform a calculation
explanation: Adleman encoded cities and edges as oligonucleotides so that base-pairing spontaneously assembled all candidate paths in parallel (on the order of 10^14 molecules in a tube), then used length selection, amplification, and sequencing to extract valid Hamiltonian paths. The power came from massive molecular parallelism, not from machine-code programmability, storage density, or replication speed.
